title: Nuclear Weapons
lead: Within seven years of the discovery of fission, the first nuclear bombs were built and used. This section describes how a fission bomb assembles a critical mass, how a thermonuclear bomb uses fission to ignite fusion, and how the energy of a nuclear explosion is measured and divided among blast, heat and radiation.
objectives: Discuss different types of fission and thermonuclear bombs.
Explain the ill effects of nuclear explosion.
summary_html:
• There are two types of nuclear weapons—fission bombs use fission alone, whereas thermonuclear bombs use fission to ignite fusion.
  • Both types of weapons produce huge numbers of nuclear reactions in a very short time.
  • Energy yields are measured in kilotons or megatons of equivalent conventional explosives and range from 0.1 kT to more than 20 MT.
  • Nuclear bombs are characterized by far more thermal output and nuclear radiation output than conventional explosives.
notes: The module prints no glossary. Five of its twelve problems have no keyed answer and are left out: the mass converted into energy by a 1.00-MT bomb, the world’s arsenal of 4,000 MT in kilowatt-hours and its value as electricity, the number and mass of plutonium-239 nuclei fissioned for a 20.0-kT yield, the height a 1.00-kT depth charge lifts an aircraft carrier, and the radiant heat of a 1.00-MT bomb at 10.0 km. As printed, the text gives Glenn Seaborg’s Nobel Prize as one in physics, and the key to the problem on a 320-kT strategic bomb writes “overheads” for warheads; both are kept.

figures.original_caption: (Figure 32.24) A gun-type fission bomb for ${}^{235}\text{U}$ utilizes two subcritical masses forced together by explosive charges inside a cannon barrel. The energy yield depends on the amount of uranium and the time it can be held together before it disassembles itself. (Figure 32.25) An implosion created by high explosives compresses a sphere of ${}^{239}\text{Pu}$ into a critical mass. The superior fissionability of plutonium has made it the universal bomb material.

This schematic of a fusion bomb (H-bomb) gives some idea of how the ${}^{239}\text{Pu}$ fission trigger is used to ignite fusion fuel. Neutrons and $\gamma$ rays transmit energy to the fusion fuel, create tritium from deuterium, and heat and compress the fusion fuel. The outer shell of ${}^{238}\text{U}$ serves to reflect some neutrons back into the fuel, causing more fusion, and it boosts the energy output by fissioning itself when neutron energies become high enough.

Approximate fractions of energy output by conventional and two types of nuclear weapons. In addition to yielding more energy than conventional weapons, nuclear bombs put a much larger fraction into thermal energy. This can be adjusted to enhance the radiation output to be more effective against troops. An enhanced radiation bomb is also called a neutron bomb.

exercises.prompt: What are some of the reasons that plutonium rather than uranium is used in all fission bombs and as the trigger in all fusion bombs?

answer.solution: Look at what makes a small, fast-assembled critical mass possible. Plutonium-239 produces more neutrons per fission than uranium-235 and is easier for a neutron to fission, so its critical mass is the smallest of any nuclide; a smaller mass makes a smaller, lighter bomb, which matters most for the trigger of a fusion bomb. Plutonium is also chemically different from uranium, so it can be separated from the uranium it is bred in, whereas ${}^{235}\text{U}$ must be separated from ${}^{238}\text{U}$ by its tiny difference in mass. The implosion design compresses the plutonium three-dimensionally and assembles the critical mass faster than the gun-type design, and the superior fissionability of plutonium has made it the universal bomb material.

exercises.prompt: Use the laws of conservation of momentum and energy to explain how a shape charge can direct most of the energy released in an explosion in a specific direction. (Note that this is similar to the situation in guns and cannons—most of the energy goes into the bullet.)

answer.solution: Treat the explosion as a push between two parts, as in a gun. The gases push equally and oppositely on the light charge facing the target and on the heavy backing behind it, so the two parts leave with momenta equal in size and opposite in direction. For the same momentum $p$, a part's kinetic energy is $p^{2}/2m$, so the light part takes far more of the energy than the heavy one. A shape charge is built so that the light, fast-moving part is aimed in one direction, inward toward the plutonium, and most of the energy released goes that way, just as most of a cannon's energy goes into the shell rather than the much heavier cannon.

exercises.prompt: How does the lithium deuteride in the thermonuclear bomb shown in Figure 32.28 supply tritium $({}^{3}\text{H})$ as well as deuterium $({}^{2}\text{H})$?

answer.solution: Lithium deuteride is a compound of lithium and deuterium, so the deuterium is already in the fuel. Neutrons from the fission trigger strike the ${}^{6}\text{Li}$ nuclei and make tritium through the reaction $n + {}^{6}\text{Li} \to {}^{3}\text{H} + {}^{4}\text{He}$. The fuel thus holds both of the nuclei needed for deuterium-tritium fusion, and the tritium is made only when the bomb goes off.

exercises.prompt: Fallout from nuclear weapons tests in the atmosphere is mainly ${}^{90}\text{Sr}$ and ${}^{137}\text{Cs}$, which have 28.6- and 32.2-y half-lives, respectively. Atmospheric tests were terminated in most countries in 1963, although China only did so in 1980. It has been found that environmental activities of these two isotopes are decreasing faster than their half-lives. Why might this be?

answer.solution: Radioactive decay alone would lower the activity of each isotope by half in one half-life, so a faster fall means the nuclei are also leaving the places where the activity is measured. Fallout settles on the surface and is then carried away: rain washes it into the soil and down into the ground water, and rivers carry it to the sea, where it is diluted. Strontium and cesium are also taken up by plants and animals and moved through food chains. Each of these removes the isotopes from the surface layers that are sampled, so the measured activity decreases faster than decay alone would make it.

exercises.prompt: Find the mass converted into energy by a 12.0-kT bomb.

answer.hint: Convert the yield to joules at $4.2\times10^{12}\ \text{J}$ per kiloton, then use $\Delta m = E/c^{2}$.

exercises.prompt: Fusion bombs use neutrons from their fission trigger to create tritium fuel in the reaction $n + {}^{6}\text{Li} \to {}^{3}\text{H} + {}^{4}\text{He}$. What is the energy released by this reaction in MeV?

answer.hint: Subtract the masses of ${}^{3}\text{H}$ and ${}^{4}\text{He}$ from those of the neutron and ${}^{6}\text{Li}$, all in u, and multiply the difference by 931.5 MeV/u.

exercises.prompt: A radiation-enhanced nuclear weapon (or neutron bomb) can have a smaller total yield and still produce more prompt radiation than a conventional nuclear bomb. This allows the use of neutron bombs to kill nearby advancing enemy forces with radiation without blowing up your own forces with the blast. For a 0.500-kT radiation-enhanced weapon and a 1.00-kT conventional nuclear bomb: (a) Compare the blast yields. (b) Compare the prompt radiation yields.

answer.solution:
(a) Blast yields $2.1\times10^{12}\ \text{J}$ to $8.4\times10^{11}\ \text{J}$, or 2.5 to 1, conventional to radiation enhanced.
(b) Prompt radiation yields $6.3\times10^{11}\ \text{J}$ to $2.1\times10^{11}\ \text{J}$, or 3 to 1, radiation enhanced to conventional.

exercises.prompt:
Assume one-fourth of the yield of a typical 320-kT strategic bomb comes from fission reactions averaging 200 MeV and the remainder from fusion reactions averaging 20 MeV.
(a) Calculate the number of fissions and the approximate mass of uranium and plutonium fissioned, taking the average atomic mass to be 238.
(b) Find the number of fusions and calculate the approximate mass of fusion fuel, assuming an average total atomic mass of the two nuclei in each reaction to be 5.
(c) Considering the masses found, does it seem reasonable that some missiles could carry 10 warheads? Discuss, noting that the nuclear fuel is only a part of the mass of a warhead.

parts.hint: A quarter of the yield, at $4.2\times10^{12}\ \text{J}$ per kiloton, divided by 200 MeV in joules.
Three quarters of the yield divided by 20 MeV in joules.

answer.solution:
(a) $1.1\times10^{25}$ fissions, 4.4 kg
(b) $3.2\times10^{26}$ fusions, 2.7 kg
(c) The nuclear fuel totals only 6 kg, so it is quite reasonable that some missiles carry 10 overheads. The mass of the fuel would only be 60 kg and therefore the mass of the 10 warheads, weighing about 10 times the nuclear fuel, would be only 1500 lbs. If the fuel for the missiles weighs 5 times the total weight of the warheads, the missile would weigh about 9000 lbs or 4.5 tons. This is not an unreasonable weight for a missile.

exercises.prompt: It is estimated that weapons tests in the atmosphere have deposited approximately 9 MCi of ${}^{90}\text{Sr}$ on the surface of the earth. Find the mass of this amount of ${}^{90}\text{Sr}$.

answer.hint: Convert the activity to becquerels, find the number of nuclei from $N = R\,t_{1/2}/0.693$ with the 28.8-y half-life, and multiply by the mass of one ${}^{90}\text{Sr}$ atom.

exercises.prompt:
One scheme to put nuclear weapons to nonmilitary use is to explode them underground in a geologically stable region and extract the geothermal energy for electricity production. There was a total yield of about 4,000 MT in the combined arsenals in 2006. If 1.00 MT per day could be converted to electricity with an efficiency of 10.0%:
(a) What would the average electrical power output be?
(b) How many years would the arsenal last at this rate?

parts.hint: One megaton is $4.2\times10^{15}\ \text{J}$; take a tenth of it and divide by the seconds in a day.
